title: Write a query to find duplicate records in a table (GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT > 1).
shortTitle: Find Duplicate Records — GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT > 1
topicTitle: Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM

s1_definition.profdef: To find duplicate records you group by the column or set of columns that defines "sameness," count the rows in each group, and keep only the groups whose count is greater than one using a `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` clause. `WHERE` cannot filter on an aggregate, so the count condition must go in `HAVING`, which filters groups after aggregation.

Priya takes every registration form, sorts them into piles by PAN number, and then only pulls out the piles that have two or more forms — those are the duplicates. Sorting into PAN piles is `GROUP BY pan`, counting each pile is `COUNT(*)`, and keeping only piles bigger than one is `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
s1_definition.oneliner: `GROUP BY` the columns that define a duplicate, then `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` — because you cannot filter an aggregate in `WHERE`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To find duplicate records you group by the column or set of columns that defines "sameness," count the rows in each group, and keep only the groups whose count is greater than one using a `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` clause. `WHERE` cannot filter on an aggregate, so the count condition must go in `HAVING`, which filters groups after aggregation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India KYC team suspects some customers registered twice with the same PAN. Priya takes every registration form, sorts them into piles by PAN number, and then only pulls out the piles that have two or more forms — those are the duplicates. Sorting into PAN piles is `GROUP BY pan`, counting each pile is `COUNT(*)`, and keeping only piles bigger than one is `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.

**One line to remember:** `GROUP BY` the columns that define a duplicate, then `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` — because you cannot filter an aggregate in `WHERE`.

sections.s2_technical:
Duplicates are defined by which columns must match. If two rows with the same email are duplicates, you group by email. If a duplicate means the same first name, last name and date of birth, you group by all three. The pattern is:

```sql
SELECT pan, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM customers
GROUP BY pan
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY cnt DESC;
```

`GROUP BY pan` buckets rows by PAN, `COUNT(*)` tallies each bucket, and `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` discards buckets that appear only once, leaving only the PANs that repeat. The reason the count condition lives in `HAVING` and not `WHERE` is fundamental to SQL's order of evaluation: `WHERE` runs before grouping, on individual rows, so at that point the group count does not exist yet. `HAVING` runs after grouping, so it can see the aggregate. Writing `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` is a syntax error.

This query tells you which values are duplicated and how many times, but it returns one row per duplicated value, not the actual duplicate rows. If you need the full offending rows (to inspect or delete), you either join back or use a window function:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT c.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pan) AS pan_count
    FROM customers c
) t
WHERE pan_count > 1
ORDER BY pan;
```

Here `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pan)` annotates every row with how many rows share its PAN, without collapsing them, so you can filter to the full set of duplicate rows.

A few important nuances. First, if the duplicate key can contain `NULL`, remember two `NULL`s are not considered equal by `GROUP BY` in some engines and the behavior around NULL grouping differs, so define whether NULLs count as duplicates. Second, for case- or whitespace-insensitive duplicates (common with emails and names), you normalize inside the group key, for example `GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))`, otherwise `Rajesh@x.com` and `rajesh@x.com ` look distinct. Third, to actually remove duplicates you typically keep the lowest id and delete the rest, often with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY id)` and delete where the row number is greater than one. Fourth, finding duplicates after the fact is reactive; the durable fix is a `UNIQUE` constraint or unique index on the key so the database refuses to insert the second copy in the first place. For performance, an index on the grouped column makes the duplicate scan far cheaper.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India discovered that some customers exist twice in the `customers` table with the same PAN because the registration flow lacked a unique constraint and two near-simultaneous sign-ups both succeeded. Before adding the constraint, the data team must first find and clean the existing duplicates. Rajesh's PAN appears twice (two customer rows), Priya's PAN appears once. The team needs a report of every PAN that occurs more than once.

This is the classic `GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` pattern. Our mini-project models a `CustomerRow` with an id and a PAN, a repository holding rows including a duplicated PAN, and a `DuplicateFinderService` that returns the PANs occurring more than once, mirroring the SQL exactly.

The code will contain: a `CustomerRow` class, a `CustomerRepository`, a `DuplicateGroup` DTO (the key plus the count), a `DuplicateFinderService.findDuplicatePans()` method implementing group-count-having, and a `Demo` that prints the duplicated PANs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three customer rows — two with PAN `ABCDE1234F` (Rajesh Kumar and Rajesh K) and one with PAN `PQRSX9876L` (Priya).

Step 1: The service reads all rows. In SQL this is the table scan the `GROUP BY` performs. Each row has an id, a name, and a PAN.

Step 2: For each row the service normalizes the PAN (trim and uppercase, mirroring `LOWER(TRIM(...))` normalization) and increments a counter keyed by that PAN. This is `COUNT(*)` grouped by PAN. After the pass, `ABCDE1234F` maps to 2 and `PQRSX9876L` maps to 1.

Step 3: The service keeps only groups whose count is greater than one. This is the `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` filter. `ABCDE1234F` survives with count 2; `PQRSX9876L` is discarded because it appears once.

Step 4: Results are sorted by count descending (`ORDER BY cnt DESC`). Only the duplicated PAN remains.

Step 5: The application prints the one duplicated PAN with its count. The data team now knows exactly which PAN to clean up before adding a unique constraint.

```
Oct 25, 2026 16:53:40 WARNING: Found 1 duplicate PAN group(s)
DUPLICATE PAN   COUNT
ABCDE1234F      2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate records I group by the column or set of columns that defines a duplicate, count the rows in each group, and keep only the groups whose count exceeds one with a HAVING clause: `SELECT pan, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY pan HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`. The reason the count condition must go in HAVING and not WHERE is SQL's evaluation order — WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, when the group count does not yet exist, whereas HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can see the count. If I need the actual duplicate rows rather than just the duplicated values, I use a window function, annotating each row with `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pan)` and filtering to rows where that is greater than one.

In our National Bank of India customer table we found some customers existed twice with the same PAN because the sign-up flow had no unique constraint and two near-simultaneous registrations both succeeded. I used this group-count-having query to list every duplicated PAN so the data team could clean them up, keeping the lowest id and deleting the rest with a ROW_NUMBER approach. The senior points I always add are that I normalize the key, for example with LOWER and TRIM on emails, so that case and whitespace variations are caught, that I must decide whether NULLs count as duplicates, and most importantly that finding duplicates is only the reactive half — the durable fix is a UNIQUE constraint or unique index on the key so the database itself refuses the second copy. The line I remember is: group by the duplicate key, then HAVING COUNT greater than one, and back it with a unique constraint so it never happens again.

---

keyPoints: GROUP BY: group rows by column values
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
HAVING: filter groups (vs WHERE which filters rows)
GROUP BY + HAVING vs WHERE: WHERE runs first, HAVING runs after grouping
